column2: A student in his thirties arrives with his supposed “wife” to study with Olson; he turns out to be violent (boasting of his fights, brandishing a knife when drunk, a wife with a bruised face). His real, pregnant wife turns up; he refuses her at first; she goes to tell her story to Travelers' Aid in Asheville, and an investigator comes to the college. Confronted, the student confesses and retorts that the director himself is living with a woman who is not his wife (Olson's divorce from Connie was not final) and that some people here sleep with other men. A chair broken over a head, a face slashed, according to his boasts; a knife brandished when drunk; a pregnant wife abandoned; Travelers' Aid in Asheville. Consequences: The risk of immorality charges and of forced closure by the state authorities, a factor, probably minor, in Olson's change of heart and the decision to close.

Early fall 1956, although a few people have already arrived for the new term, Huss and Olson go to Asheville, sit down in a café, and agree to close: a tiny enrollment, a faculty reduced to the two of them (Dan Rice having agreed to come back to replace Fiore), and only Huss wanting to teach. Alternatives considered and rejected: Tony Landreau's mobile university (selling all the assets), becoming Channel 2's “University of the Air,” or persuading Paul Williams to rent a floor of a Manhattan skyscraper. Consequences: It was time to go, time to do a new thing (Huss, fifteen years later).

Fiore leaves for New York; Huss and the cast of Medea leave with Duncan for San Francisco; Olson stays on for a while in exchange for housing to see the college through the final ordeal of closing. Everyone has to leave within thirty days; some overstay the deadline. Weinberger remembers how the feeling of community evaporated once the decision was made. The usual farewell drink with Olson before getting into the cars. Consequences: The end of the college; everyone scatters to his destination.

Shortly after arriving in San Francisco, the company breaks up: the star leaves, Duncan reconnects with his old friends, Huss takes part in a Quaker project to relocate Indians into industrial jobs. Many stay on, hanging out in a bar run by Knute Stiles and Leo Krikorian (Black Mountain alumni) and sometimes quarreling with Ginsberg's circle. Ginsberg finds them diabolical, suicidal, hung up on authority like Ezra Pound, and professional “cocksmen”; Corso calls them “mental gangsters,” “hip squares” cultivating a “deliberate lack of enthusiasm.”

Williams writes to all of Olson's friends: $25 in exchange for their name in the colophon. Twenty-five subscribers cover about 60% of a production cost of about $1,000; a printing of 350 copies at $3, sold out in three or four years. $25 per subscriber; 25 subscribers; cost ~$1,000; 350 copies; $3 a copy Consequences: Publication by Jargon

Jonathan Williams writes to all of Olson's friends: a $25 contribution in exchange for having their name printed in the book's colophon; twenty-five people subscribe. 25 subscribers, about 60% of a production cost of about $1,000; a printing of 350 copies at $3 each, sold over three to four years

Creeley, in Mallorca, no doubt with Olson's encouragement, publishes “The Pipe” in No. 6, spring 1956, of the Black Mountain Review, without payment. No. 6, spring 1956, no payment Consequences: For Rumaker, it was worth all the gold in the world
In 1956, Wieners will find a second master at Black Mountain in Robert Duncan.

One early spring afternoon, the group goes on a picnic north into the mountains. On the way back, caught in a terrible storm in the deep forest, drenched instantly, they dance defiantly in the mud amid the lightning and thunder, laughing, unafraid. Soaked to the bone, a muddy path, tall trees, deafening thunderclaps, lightning crackling all around Consequences: One fear lost in this wild nature, where they feel truly charmed

Earlier in the 1956 summer session, Duncan's satirical play against Olson, “The Origin of Old Son,” was performed, with the muscular ex-Marine Jerry Van de Wiele as a baby, in a bonnet and baby clothes in a stroller, playing Charles: a new and wicked declaration of Duncan's independence from Olson. Jerry, a lively source of pointed gossip, tells Rumaker that things are tense between the two men. A stroller, a bonnet, and baby clothes Consequences: Tense relations between Charles and Duncan; Rumaker does not meet Duncan, away for a few days, but will see him in September in Philadelphia
Ruth Kligman, Pollock's mistress, spends his last days with him and survives the car crash that kills him. Consequences: Pollock dies at the height of his fame, according to Kligman

Pollock dies in a car accident; at the Cedar, the artists disagree: suicide, the culmination of his violence, or the argument that sobriety killed him. Consequences: De Kooning becomes the undisputed king of Abstract Expressionism; he takes up with Pollock's companion, Ruth Kligman.

A one-man show of abstract urban landscapes: a dealer's dream, a resounding commercial success, attracting the right enemies, according to Elaine, and the collectors. Bill is 52; photographed and filmed Consequences: Bill becomes a critical and financial star

The birth of Lisa, daughter of Bill and Joan Ward. Elaine, visiting, noticed that Joan had registered as “Mrs. de Kooning” and let drop that she and Bill had always wanted a child, a remark that went around the art world. Elaine, 38, had just had a hysterectomy. Consequences: Lisa's birth precipitates the separation

Shortly after the birth, Joan was showing the child to friends when Bill arrived quietly, smiling, rocking on his heels; Joan understood that he would be a good father and stopped worrying. Bill smiling behind the visitors, rocking on his heels

Ruth, Pollock's former companion, injured in the fatal accident, rebuilds her life; one evening, elegantly dressed, she runs into Bill and Elaine dining together in a restaurant on the Lower East Side; at a New Year's party, she declares that they have really met, a great love. According to one artist's wife, this affair proves that Bill has buried Jackson; he boasts of having had her. An elegant dress, dinner, a New Year's party Consequences: Bill changes for Ruth: a trip to Europe, dressing up, buying her clothes and trinkets

A solo show that attracts attention but invites comparison with Bill; Art News ranks it among the ten best of the year. Consequences: Contributes more to her teaching career than to major international exhibitions

A 495-page documentary novel about the Leopold-Loeb case, which Levin calls “the crime of our century.” Goodman judges it good: a serious selection of journalistic, medical, and legal material, often verbatim, with a touching involvement of the narrator. Price: $5. 495 pages, $5, Simon and Schuster Consequences: Grounds for Goodman's comparison with Dreiser

A few weeks after the start of the semester, Albers prowls the room in silence and pockets every eraser he finds; Horowitz hides his, but Albers spots his propped elbow and pulls it away without a word to forbid him to rest his chin in his hand, then straightens the pad on which Horowitz is drawing lines meant to be vertical. Erasers pocketed in silence; an elbow tugged; a pad straightened. Consequences: Horowitz feels intimidated but eager to please Albers.

Huff, a Yale architecture graduate holding a Fulbright for the HfG in 1956, tells Albers that he is going to study with Vordemberge-Gildewart; Albers then becomes more vocal about his opinion of the artist. Fulbright scholarship.

President Griswold, knowing that Sawyer would not be coming back either, overrides the mandatory retirement rule and asks Albers to stay on two more years as chairman of the Department of Design; Albers negotiates three days a week instead of four and delegates his color and drawing courses to his assistants. Assistants named: Sillman, Kloszewski, Welliver; he plans to visit these classes occasionally Consequences: Albers stays on until 1958 as chairman and until 1961 as a teacher
Albers writes “A Method of Teaching Color Based on Training in Visual Perception,” a statement attached to a grant application to the Rockefeller Foundation.
In 1956, Duncan teaches by working at length first on vowel sounds, then on consonant clusters, then on syllables, working the materials of poetry, perhaps with Albers's work in mind.

A photograph taken to mark the announcement of the closing: sixteen people crowded onto a couch and the floor in what seems to be Olson's cabin; most are not looking at the camera; Olson stares owlishly into the lens; two figures in beatnik black, he leaning to the left, she reaching for a pack of cigarettes. A boy drinking tea; a cigarette already in hand; a table with a pack of cigarettes Consequences: An image of the social, political, and sexual distance taken from the college's founding; it foreshadows the upheavals of the 1960s

Fiore leaves the college ten years after his arrival, among the last of a dilapidated community holed up in ramshackle cabins; with Rice, King, Fick, Field, and Van de Wiele, he forms the last group of painters from a college that, by the mid-1950s, was turning mainly toward writing. Ramshackle cabins; Fiore's studies funded by the GI Bill; a rise from student to teacher in three years.

In a widely circulated photograph, Asawa sits on a stool amid her hanging sculptures, in the same corner of the house; behind her the blackboard, once covered with scribbles, has been conspicuously wiped clean. A stool, hanging sculptures, a clean blackboard Consequences: Motherhood is censored, literally erased, to fit a model of artistic meaning
The store shows “Japanese household objects” alongside Asawa's sculptures, without distinguishing the functional from the aesthetic. A modernist design store

Christensen commissions a looped-wire sculpture for her dance studio; according to Jenelle Porter, the commission explains why the piece matches the interior height of the studio. A 1956 photograph shows Christensen with her students, children among them, around the work. Untitled (S.437), 1956, Santa Barbara; semitransparent surfaces; windows on eucalyptus and hills Consequences: The work's constant presence in the studio, mediating dancing bodies, glass architecture, and the California landscape.

Christensen commissions from Asawa a looped-wire sculpture (Untitled S.437) for her dance studio; according to Jenelle Porter, the commission explains why the work matches the interior height of the studio. A 1956 photograph: Christensen with her students, mothers and children, under the sculpture; semitransparent surfaces mediating dancing bodies, glass architecture, and the California landscape (eucalyptus, hills). Consequences: The sculpture remains permanently suspended in the studio.

A gelatin silver print titled Eggs in Ruth Asawa's Basket, 9½ × 7½ inches, which literalizes the egg baskets seen in Toluca Gelatin silver print, 9½ × 7½ in., collection of the Imogen Cunningham Trust
Duncan teaches at the college in the spring and summer of 1956.
Duncan's play “Medea at Kolchis; or The Maiden Head” premieres at Black Mountain College in 1956 and is published by Oyez in 1965.

After two years in St. Louis, a move to the San Francisco Bay Area; in 1956, he forms Marquis & Stoller with the young architect Robert B. Marquis, son of Lucian Marquis. An office on Beach Street; a general practice of architecture and planning (residential, housing, institutional, governmental). An office on Beach Street; the use of natural materials, the influence of Marcel Breuer and of Albers's courses

Student recruitment has collapsed; the last registrar, Connie Spencer, has left the college and her common-law husband Charles Olson. Eloise Mixon, a student, spends a few hours a week reading and sometimes answering inquiries; she answers Ebbe, enclosing a fake brochure created in the desperate hope of regaining GI status. A fictitious brochure: a list of courses and how they were supposed to work, according to Borregaard Consequences: Ebbe is admitted

Neck-high grass; visitors guided along the paths; kudzu overrunning the two lodges and the faculty cabins; the Studies Building on a shaky foundation, the coal bin collapsed, broken windows replaced with cardboard and tape; garbage piled in six-foot mounds; the library looted; the pot shop padlocked; the print shop barely working; the wood shop rented to Don Mixon, who hardly uses it and never pays rent; the Science Building abandoned; the farm forgotten, the farmhouse empty; the last washing machine gives up the ghost with a sign above it reading FUCKT. Mounds of garbage six feet high; a sign in capitals: FUCKT; kudzu

The first issue of Liberation listed the ills neglected by liberals: war, poverty, boredom, authoritarianism. Boredom referred to urban anomie, public relations, mass communications, the suburban standard of living; authoritarianism referred to top-down leadership in parties, corporations, unions, families, and schools, democracy reduced to democracy by consent.

Tannenbaum writes to the dean of the College that he has felt very alone in this undertaking; the whole thing is too irregular to fit the University's traditional forms of funding; without support, it could all be nipped in the bud. Consequences: A revelation of the movement's financial precariousness
Designs the whole production of Nocturnes.
Costumes for 3 Epitaphs, 4 Epitaphs, and Untitled Duet; sound track and costumes for The Least Flycatcher, premiered at the Henry Street Settlement Playhouse. Magnetic tape as score

Jouffroy publicly rejects all political and moral responsibility, holding that moral judgment is almost always negative or ineffective and belongs only to those who value freedom only to deny it to themselves and others. Consequences: Moral judgment serves to justify collective inaction, the “wait and see” of those who have forgotten to change the world.

A few weeks after Front unique, Jouffroy answers Estienne with a similar refutation of Surrealism, invoking the resistance to torture and state executions shown at the Anti-procès, notably in the work by Matta placed at the center of the exhibition and in the play performed for the occasion. A work by Matta at the center of the exhibition; a play performed at the event Consequences: The argument that the withdrawal of judgment is itself an act of subversion; moral judgment would concern only oppressive regimes and café revolutionaries.

In the fall of 1956, Olson and Huss agree to begin closing the college. Olson stays at Lake Eden to oversee the property sales and the continued academic programs, with the vision of a dispersed university of satellite programs throughout the world. Consequences: Robert Duncan and students carry on the theater workshop in which he wrote and staged Medea: The Maidenhead.
After his military service, Dawson visits the college: sad, lost, with no Olson walking about, no more order, his secret places turned into a deserted jungle. Consequences: The college closes in 1957

Kepes invites Fuller to contribute to his visual compilation book, which synthesizes scientific and aesthetic knowledge around the motif of patterns of organization; it includes the geodesic dome, objects by the Eameses, Le Corbusier's Modulor, and microscopic images of nature (snail shells). Images: the geodesic dome, works by the Eameses, Le Corbusier's modular figure, microscopic and enlarged images of snails

Kepes assembles a visual companion book that seeks to synthesize and systematize all scientific and aesthetic knowledge around the notion of organizational structuring; he includes images of Fuller's geodesic dome and of other inventions of his. The book also contains objects by Charles and Ray Eames, Le Corbusier's Modulor, and microscopic images of nature: snails' tongues, the Crab Nebula. Consequences: Fuller appears there among the examples of a harmonious unity of nature based on repetition and network structure.

Observers note that Black Mountain College did not really end in 1956 but dispersed: groups of former students meet in New York and San Francisco in small, friendly communities exchanging ideas about music, theater, fiction, and art. Olson and the poets of the Black Mountain Review of the 1950s become the “Black Mountain poets.” Consequences: The birth of a school of poetry and of a lasting network

Erwin Panofsky, the great specialist in the iconography of the Northern Renaissance, rarely turns to modernism; he writes that Klee shows Pandora's box as a vase of flowers from which evil vapors escape through an opening clearly evoking the female genitals.

An exhibition of thirty-two paintings by Renoir, the occasion for Elaine de Kooning's essay “Renoir: As If by Magic.” 32 paintings; dominant tones of gray and cool blue, few red hues; compressive rather than expansive paintings Consequences: The birth of the essay

Elaine paints Bill frontally, knees bent, thighs spread in a sharp triangle; she erases his features in a drawing and, in Bill at St. Marks, struggles for a long time, changing the color, changing the shoulders, before blocking out his face with a patch of blue and spraying one arm in a blue mist Words: Bill had become an angry man; it was oppressive (Elaine) Atmosphere: Pictorial rancor, a hard frontal body beneath the mist Stakes: The marriage comes apart in painting a year before the actual separation

Williams and Creeley arrive with Zukofsky's inscribed book. Pound is sitting on the lawn among his faithful. Dorothy Pound comes to ask who they are; they explain; Pound sends back his refusal: no friends of Charles Olson. The two visitors leave in shame. Words: Pound to his wife: he does not want to see friends of Charles Olson. Williams: they slunk away Atmosphere: Embarrassed tension, a hostile court around the confined poet Stakes: A book meant as a bridge between poets refused; Olson's shadow reaches even the hospital lawn

While rehearsals of Medea have been going on for months, Duncan, sitting in the Mixons' living room, writes one of the longest speeches in the play while keeping up an intermittent conversation with four or five people present. Atmosphere: Cagean simultaneity: writing and chatter interwoven. Stakes: The text literally fits the actors, like a too-tight glove.

A pregnant woman arrives, declaring that she is the wife of the student and has come to take him back; he refuses; she goes to Travelers' Aid in Asheville to say that she has been abandoned for another woman at a crazy school; an investigator comes to the college; confronted, the student confesses and turns the accusation against the administration. Words: What difference does it make? The head of the place is living with a woman who is not his wife too, and some guys here sleep with other guys. Atmosphere: The threat of an immorality scandal that could lead to forced closure by the state. Stakes: One of the causes, minor but real, of the decision to close.

In early fall 1956, they sit down in a café and review the situation: a tiny enrollment, a faculty reduced to the two of them, only Huss wanting to teach; the alternatives (a mobile university, television, a skyscraper) are reviewed and rejected. Words: Huss: it was time to go, time to do a new thing (recalled fifteen years later, sadly). Atmosphere: Lucid, melancholy resignation. Stakes: The college's death decided by two men, quietly.

Once the decision is made, everyone takes his car, usually after a farewell drink with Olson, and scatters; a few overstay the thirty-day deadline. Words: Weinberger: the feeling of community evaporated once the decision was made. Atmosphere: It was as simple as that, heartbreakingly simple. Stakes: An unceremonious end to a twenty-three-year adventure.

Coming back from an early spring picnic, the group is caught in a terrible storm and drenched instantly. Instead of fleeing, they dance gaily in the mud of the path under the tall trees, laughing amid the thunder and lightning, with no apparent fear. Atmosphere: Giddy defiance, laughter, crackling lightning, layer upon layer of water and mud Stakes: One more fear lost in the wilderness; the protective charm of Black Mountain

The artists learn of Pollock's death in a car accident; interpretations fly: suicide, the inevitable outcome of his violence, or deadly sobriety Atmosphere: Stupefaction, speculation Stakes: The end of the rivalry; de Kooning becomes the undisputed king

Visiting after Lisa's birth, Elaine notices “Mrs. de Kooning” in the register and lets drop her witticism, which will go around the art world Words: Oh, she and Bill had always wanted a child Atmosphere: Wounded elegance, irony as a mask for pain Stakes: Elaine refuses to give up her place as wife

Joan shows the pretty baby to admiring friends; Bill arrives without a sound, smiling, rocking on his heels behind the group; Joan understands that he would be all right as a father Atmosphere: Quiet, tender happiness Stakes: Bill's acceptance of fatherhood

Albers prowls the room in silence, pocketing every eraser; Horowitz hides his; Albers comes up behind him, tugs his elbow without a word to forbid his chin-in-hand, then straightens his pad of vertical lines. Words: No words: an entirely gestural, silent correction. Atmosphere: Silence, vigilance, fear of being spotted mixed with admiration. Stakes: The master's power: to see everything, correct everything, without a word.

Huff announces that he is going to Ulm on his Fulbright to study with Vordemberge-Gildewart; Albers pounces: why? one cannot learn structure from him; then he portrays him jumping on the de Stijl bandwagon, flag in hand; as Huff is leaving the office, a last arrow: do not study with him, he is scrambled, better to study Swabian Baroque Words: “Why? You cannot learn structure from him”; “He is scrambled. Better you should study Schwabian Baroque” Atmosphere: Stinging tartness, an exit from the office punctuated by a final warning Stakes: Albers's aesthetic loyalties and his clear-cut enmities

Sixteen people squeezed onto a couch and the floor to mark the announcement of the closing; almost no one looks at the lens; each looks at someone else, out of frame, or at the floor; Olson stares at the camera; behind, a boy in black leans to the left, perhaps toward a boy drinking tea; a girl in black reaches for a pack of cigarettes. Atmosphere: Fatigue, defiance, detachment; tea, cigarettes, beatnik black Stakes: The end of a community that foreshadows the 1960s

A photo session in a corner of the house: Asawa sitting on a stool, surrounded by her hanging creations; in a widely circulated version, the blackboard behind her, once covered with scribbles, has been wiped clean. Atmosphere: Light, the transparency of the wires dissolving at the brightest point Stakes: A literal censorship of motherhood to establish artistic legitimacy
Schweikher, a besieged chairman, resigns in February 1956 and leaves Yale at the end of the semester. Consequences: The question of Albers's successor becomes moot

Jonathan Williams writes to Dawson that he will publish the second volume of the Maximus Letters (11-22) and asks him for a drawing of Olson for the announcement, to accompany a statement by W.C. Williams. Dawson shows the letter to Kline and draws Olson from memory, in a few tries, on paper with ink and a brush provided by Kline, who approves: “Pretty good!” Paper, ink, brush; a couple of tries; the drawing reproduced on the book's cover Consequences: The drawing is used for the announcement of the volume and for the cover of the Black Mountain Book

Dawson shows Jonathan's letter and says he can draw Olson from memory; Kline gives him paper, ink, and a brush; after a few tries the drawing is done and shown. Words: Kline, smiling: “Pretty good!” Atmosphere: A lesson in understatement, studio camaraderie Stakes: Black Mountain's legacy in the New York that came after

In early spring 1956, the college rents the lower campus as a boys' camp with a resolutely Christian orientation, which opens in the summer of 1956; the “saints” below and the “sinners” above cross paths in comic scenes: Van de Wiele sometimes hitches a ride to Asheville with the counselors and has to bite his lip when they say of a camper, in their Southern accent: “He is a wonderful, true little Christian and mah heart goes out to him”, which the sinners translate as: he's a little bastard.

An elaborate fifteen-page “Bulletin,” apparently intended mainly to impress the V.A., with group divisions on “The American Language” and “The Western Tradition” and course titles such as “Pre-Homeric Literature and Culture” and “Theocritus”; in reality, most of the work of 1955-1956 is done in tutorials: each person asks another's opinion of a painting, a text, a manuscript, an idea. 15 pages, learned course titles Consequences: The gap between the institutional showcase and the tutorial reality.
Takes part in the annual exhibition.

At dusk, Rumaker, in a blue mood, sits for hours on the dusty wooden steps, knees against his chest, projecting his loneliness onto the trees disappearing into the darkness climbing the hillsides; he envies the starry skies and would like to lose himself in them. He thinks the house is empty (Laurie and Naomi were in fact in their upstairs apartment). Dusty wooden steps; several hours without moving; total darkness fallen when the car arrives; Olson's expression: “sucking the cock of your own experience”

Tom, drunk and angry after the evening at Ma Peak's, refuses to stop at Black Dwarf, where he visibly drops no one off (Jorge stays aboard), zigzags across the field with the doors flapping, the passengers shouting and trying to grab the wheel; he shouts “If this is what you want, you're getting it!” and crashes into the fieldstone chimney right next to the steps from which Rumaker has just dashed inside. A Buick, the pedal no doubt floored; open doors flapping; cries of “Tom! Tom!”; “Aw, Tom come on” (Jorge); no visible blood despite the violence of the impact Consequences: The chimney only chipped; the whole house shaken; several injured

Tom, slumped over the wheel, mutters that he had warned them; Rumaker frees him, his legs pinned under the dashboard; Dan, unconscious, his face ashen, is carried in and laid on the lobby “daybed”; Jorge, relatively unhurt, walks in small circles on the grass, holding his head in his hands. Laurie and Naomi come down wide-eyed; Olson, Huss, Chamberlain with the newly arrived Elaine, Joe Fiore (and perhaps Mary) appear. A pink and pale pink blanket with white and yellow stripes, needing a wash, thrown by Tom over an old sour mattress; Dan laid on the bed; Dan's back feared broken Consequences: The decision to call for help from the pay phone in the Studies Building

Creeley seizes Rumaker's hand, pulls him down onto the edge of the bed, and talks without being able to stop, not about the accident but about his wife and himself, tears running down without his wiping them, repeating “You're a lovely man, Mike” and “Tom is a lovely man”; beneath it all Rumaker hears only forgive me. Rumaker, embarrassed and furious, keeps quiet and listens: it was the only kindness he could do him. A surprisingly strong handgrip; a hoarse, rapid voice, the throat seeming to choke with rage, fear, and hurt Consequences: Rumaker will later learn that the teasing of Tom by Creeley, Dan, and Jorge was the main cause of the drama

To avoid legal trouble, and given the college's bad image in the Swannanoa valley and in North Carolina, they decide to say that the accelerator pedal stuck. State troopers arrive in a car with a flashing light, in “Smokey the Bear” hats, take flash photographs of the Buick crumpled like an accordion against the chimney, and fill out a report. Gray-blue uniforms with shiny buttons, gun belts with holsters; the bare bulb over the front door; an accident on private property, hence little risk

After the injured and the police have left, a few people talk until late; left alone, Mary and Joe give Rumaker, at the end of his nerves, some tea, then go walking with him near the lake. At dawn they cross back over the wooden footbridge over the ravine toward Streamside, Mary turning the event over in her slow, careful way, without condemnation; Joe follows, a real and strong presence. Tea in the kitchen; leaves brightening in the early morning light; the Buick already removed (by Percy Justus and his brother, garage owners on the Black Mountain road); Mary and Joe climb back up to Minimum House

Mary and Rumaker visit Tom and Dan in that vast complex of military barracks with factory chimneys. Tom, with a broken leg, chatty and cheerful as a cricket, a former army stretcher-bearer, feels at home, denies how serious it is, and promises to manage on crutches; the accident seems to have freed him, as if he had proved his manhood. Dan, with a dislocated back, stays in the hospital a long time, then wears a back brace; Creeley, with a badly wrenched shoulder, is not hospitalized. Injuries: Tom a broken leg, Dan a dislocated back, Creeley a wrenched shoulder, Jorge almost unhurt

During the last summer session, Duncan mischievously stages The Origins of Old Sun, in which the adult protagonist in diapers, played by the painting student Gerald Van de Wiele, alludes to Olson's patriarchal theory of gender (solar masculinity, lunar femininity) and to the actual fertility of the past half decade.

Dusk: Rumaker slumped on the steps for hours. The roar of an engine echoing, headlights cutting through the branches, dust. An abrupt stop at Black Dwarf, slamming doors, shouts of argument. The car takes off again, zigzagging across the field, doors flapping, passengers yelling and clawing at Tom's shoulders to reach the wheel. Rumaker, paralyzed like a hypnotized animal, leaps at the last moment behind the French doors, near the chimney. The dull shock of metal on stone; the whole house shakes. Afterward: Jorge circling on the grass, moans from the back seat, Tom at the wheel in the greenish glow of the dashboard; Rumaker frees his legs; Dan lifeless on the daybed; the neighbors arrive; a call from the pay phone in the Studies Building; troopers, flash photographs, the invention of the stuck pedal, the injured taken away; then tea and a walk by the lake with Mary and Joe until dawn. Words: Tom: if this is what they want, they'll get it!; he had told them to stop, told them he would do it; Creeley: “You're a lovely man, Mike,” “Tom is a lovely man”; Jorge: “Aw, Tom come on”; Rumaker asks Tom whether he has broken anything; Tom doesn't think so; his legs are stuck Atmosphere: A black night, headlights in the dust, steam and smoke from the engine, a bare bulb, the greenish glow of the dashboard, a frozen silence after the impact, then a dazed crowd in a dark circle behind the police Stakes: The culmination of the last summer's tensions; death narrowly missed for Rumaker; an omen of the closing
Anni unexpectedly discovers a backstrap loom in the village of Santo Tomás, “an interesting variety of the usual kind” (letter to John Cohen, November 14, 1956). They meet Thornton Wilder.
Anni discovers a backstrap loom in Santo Tomás, “an interesting variety of the usual kind” (letter to John Cohen, November 14, 1956). They meet Thornton Wilder.

A trip in July-August; Anni discovers a backstrap loom in the village of Santo Tomás, “an interesting variety of the usual kind” (letter to John Cohen, November 14, 1956); they meet Thornton Wilder A backstrap loom in Santo Tomás

A fire destroys the Wanamaker department store; Bill, like other artists in the neighborhood, watches the flames devour the familiar landmark, hence The Time of the Fire (1956). The fire of July 1956, between West 8th and West 10th Streets Consequences: Inspires The Time of the Fire (1956)

Sawyer is pushed out with little recognition for his decade of work, allowed to resign with an appearance of dignity; he leaves for the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. A new dean will be named only two years later

On the ninth trip, Anni discovers in the village a backstrap loom that she describes to John Cohen in November as “an interesting variety of the usual kind” Words: Anni: “an interesting variety of the usual kind” Atmosphere: A textile ethnologist's curiosity Stakes: A continuity between the village weavers and her own art

Elaine meets Pollock's mother, 81, whose possessiveness reminds her of Cornelia, Bill's mother. She joins Bill on Martha's Vineyard in the sculptor David Slivka's rented house; the proximity of Joan Ward, Bill's mistress, provokes confrontations, including a quarrel over fake wedding rings (“It's no phonier than yours”). Elaine then leaves for Provincetown. Elaine had taken to answering Cornelia's letters by inventing messages from Bill

On the first day of vacation, he takes the Pennsylvania Railroad from 30th Street Station to Washington, then the Southern Railway to North Carolina (the Jim Crow cars have disappeared since his first trip in 1952). He thinks of the return as a homecoming and of Olson as a father who might set him back on the right path. He is lodged again at Meadows Inn. Segregated cars gone between 1952 and 1956; clean mountain air against the smoke and grime of Philadelphia Consequences: The dark experiences of the summer of 1955 fade

Olson invites Rumaker to supper with him and “Bet” and to see the new baby. Betty, poor, had had the child alone in a cheap room in Manhattan, the newborn first sleeping in a dresser drawer for lack of a crib; her thoughts of music and theater are on hold. Olson serves cocktails; annoyed at the poor quality of the present students, he cheerfully proposes that the remaining faculty vote to take down the college sign above the Gatehouse entrance and hoist a bright red flag bearing “SECONAL” in big letters. Seeing Rumaker talking nonstop, he leans toward Betty and murmurs ironically: “See? Genius.” A baby born in May 1955, named Charles Peter; a bright red flag; the word “SECONAL” Consequences: The three chat merrily until class time

Rumaker, ashamed of his bad front teeth (neglect due to poverty and fear of dentists; his last visit dates from the emergency at Black Mountain with Charles), unconsciously puts his hand in front of his mouth when he talks, a gesture taken from his mother, also ashamed of her teeth ruined by poverty. Olson catches the gesture immediately and asks with a slight smile: “What's the matter with your mouth?” Consequences: Rumaker takes his hand away: he knows nothing can be hidden from Charles, neither bad writing nor bad teeth

Because of the heat of the dog days, Olson holds his writing class in the basement conference room of the Studies Building: half a dozen students or more around the big square table, almost the entire student population, even smaller than when Rumaker left. Olson, with high-flown praise (perhaps a little lubricated), asks Rumaker, an old hand, to comment on a student's little poem. Rumaker, overwhelmed, can find nothing to criticize but the British spellings. Olson is visibly disappointed. The big square table; half a dozen students Consequences: Rumaker has lost his thread and his edge after a year in Philadelphia

The student in question: a handsome young blond man with black-rimmed glasses, a pot smoker and Seconal swallower, who rides his Lambretta several afternoons a week to his shrink in Asheville and later declares himself 18th in line of succession to the British throne (after a brief spell at an English public school). Rumaker falls for him at once, spends his stay circling around him, even rides on the back of the scooter all the way to Asheville, waits for him in front of the psychiatrist's office, using the wind as a pretext to wrap his arms around him and nestle against his shoulder blades. Mary Fiore photographs Rumaker astride the Lambretta in front of Meadows Inn, where Gavin also lodges. A Lambretta scooter; black-rimmed glasses; a photograph by Mary Fiore Consequences: A new obsessive love for Rumaker

Jerry later tells Rumaker that the behavior of some students, especially under alcohol or drugs (and sometimes sober), was so unpredictable that he hid his woodsplitting ax every time someone knocked at his door at Next-to-the-Last-Chance (the apartment Rumaker had shared with Merrill), for fear of possible violence. A woodsman's ax; the Next-to-the-Last-Chance apartment Consequences: A sign of the sordid, unpredictable atmosphere on campus

Rumaker, seeing that there is nothing left for him at the college in its downward spiral, thinks of hitchhiking to join Tom Field and other Black Mountaineers settled in San Francisco. He takes the train north with Jonathan Williams, who is going to New York and saves their seats with records and manuscripts from his Jargon Press. They spend almost the whole trip to Greensboro in the bar car; when they come back, two tipsy farmers in overalls and plaid shirts are occupying their seats, sitting on the records and manuscripts, apparently without noticing, and refuse to move. Jonathan, furious and stiff, retrieves his property by force; Rumaker, tipsy, is secretly amused: a fitting conclusion to his last visit. Overalls and plaid shirts; the bar car; a change at Greensboro Consequences: Getting off hungover at 30th Street early the next morning, Rumaker understands that the end of the college is near

Olson catches Rumaker in front of the cottage and invites him to supper and to see the baby; he immediately notices Rumaker's hand over his mouth. Betty proudly shows off Charles Peter before going to see to dinner. Charles makes the cocktails; all three grow merry; Olson mocks his students and proposes the red “SECONAL” flag; seeing Rumaker rattle on endlessly, he murmurs to Betty “See? Genius.”; Rumaker stops for a moment, then starts up again all the more, the three of them chatting until class time. Words: “What's the matter with your mouth?” — “See? Genius.” — the proposal to hoist “a bright red flag that says 'SECONAL'” in place of the college sign Atmosphere: Drink, gaiety, mocking tenderness, an underlying bitterness about the college's decline Stakes: A last family evening around Olson before the college's death throes

After supper, Olson seats Rumaker as guest of honor at the big square table and, after high-flown praise, has him comment on the little poem of a handsome blond in dark glasses who rides a Lambretta to his shrink. Rumaker, nervous, out of practice, no doubt tipsy, can find only a remark about British spellings; Olson is visibly disappointed. Words: Olson to Rumaker, beforehand: to show them a thing or two; Gavin will later call himself 18th in line of succession to the British throne Atmosphere: Dog-day heat, a basement, the unease of the outdated veteran Stakes: Rumaker measured against the master and found to have slipped; the college reduced to half a dozen students

Rumaker rides precariously on the scooter behind Gavin to Asheville and waits docilely in front of the psychiatrist's office during the session; the pleasure of the ride: wrapping his arms around him and nestling against his shoulder blades on the pretext of protecting himself from the wind. Atmosphere: Wind, the vibration of the scooter, bottled-up desire Stakes: A substitute obsessive love on a dying campus

Williams saves their seats with Jargon Press records and manuscripts; the two men spend the trip in the bar car; when they come back, two tipsy farmers in overalls are occupying the seats, sitting on the records without realizing it, and refuse to move; Williams retrieves his property by force, stiff with fury, while Rumaker, euphoric, sees it as a fitting end. Atmosphere: Bar-car drinking, slapstick, a morning hangover at 30th Street Stakes: A grotesque farewell to the college

Horowitz walks to Street Hall for his first Basic Drawing class; Albers announces that the course will be a course in seeing and thinking, not in imitating the Old Masters. A silent room (“hushed room”); for Horowitz the course takes on the character of The Pilgrim's Progress. Consequences: A founding experience that changes Horowitz irrevocably and pushes him toward teaching.
In his opening remarks, Albers says he is glad to see so many people wanting to learn to draw and not just to look at naked boys and girls.

Once accepted, he packs his meager belongings and hitchhikes from Virginia to Black Mountain, arriving in late September 1956, before the start of fall classes. Hitchhiking from Virginia; meager belongings
On his first full day, students take him into town and teach him to steal food from the A&P supermarket. A&P
On his first night, he joins students and teachers at Ma Peak's, the local bar just outside the town of Black Mountain. A bar just outside town
